warmup.q: fun makeCounter(): () -> Int { var count = 0; return { ++count } }. Four threads share one counter and call it 250,000 times each. What does the next call return?
options: It doesn't compile: Kotlin, like Java, won't let a lambda change a captured local
Often less than 1,000,001, and a different number from run to run
Always 250,001, because each thread gets its own copy of count
warmup.why: Kotlin does let a lambda change a captured var. It moves count into a heap object, a Ref$IntRef with one plain int field, that all four threads share. ++count is a read, an add and a write on that field, so increments get lost when two threads read the same old value. Java would refuse to compile the same code; Kotlin compiles it, and it races. The last section shows the box and the lost counts.

opening:
Picture a box of recipe cards in a kitchen drawer. You can take a card out, lend it to a friend, or lay three cards in a row for tonight's dinner. Or pin a note to one: "my oven runs hot, take five minutes off". A card is a thing you hold, not only something you do.

Code can hold its rules the same way. The last lesson, on pure functions, ended with every rule as a function we called by name. That works until each guest at your table needs different checks, and the method that checks dishes grows one if per guest.

The trap waits on the other side. A function value can carry a note from the place it was made. When that note is a variable that changes, everyone who holds the card shares it. Two threads (two paths of work running at once) writing on one note lose marks, and Kotlin compiles that without a word.

In this lesson, we'll turn checks into values, write them four ways, see what a lambda becomes on the JVM, and find the shared box inside a closure. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a drawer of recipe cards and a dinner party whose checks were stuck inside one method. Each check became a value you can store and line up per guest, and a closure kept its note from where it was made. Then the picture broke: a closure's note isn't copied, it's one shared box.

Search your Kotlin code for a var declared just before a lambda that runs somewhere else, inside submit { }, thread { } or a callback. Each one is a note several threads may write on.

Next, we'll write functions that take functions and hand them back. How do you write a retry loop once, for every call that might fail?

sections.h: Making a check a value you can hold: function types
sections.html:
Here's a dinner party in code. The host has a few dishes in mind and a few guests to please. A Dish knows its name, how many minutes it takes, its diet (vegan, vegetarian or meat), its main ingredient and whether it has nuts. Before cooking, one method checks a dish against a guest's needs:

Java
static String check(Dish d, Guest g) {
    if (d.minutes() > 60) return "too-slow";
    if (!AUTUMN.contains(d.main())) return "out-of-season";
    if (g.vegetarian() && d.diet().equals("meat")) return "has-meat";
    if (g.nutAllergy() && d.nuts()) return "has-nuts";
    // ...one more line for every guest with a need of their own
    return null;
}
Kotlin
fun check(d: Dish, g: Guest): String? {
    if (d.minutes > 60) return "too-slow"
    if (d.main !in AUTUMN) return "out-of-season"
    if (g.vegetarian && d.diet == "meat") return "has-meat"
    if (g.nutAllergy && d.nuts) return "has-nuts"
    // ...one more line for every guest with a need of their own
    return null
}

Every new need means editing this method, and every guest with a need of their own adds another flag. You can't test one check on its own, reorder them, or let a guest's settings pick which ones apply, because the checks aren't things you can hold. They're lines of code. And the guest list only ever grows.

So make each check a value, like a card in the drawer. In Kotlin a function has a type, written with an arrow: (Dish) -> Problem? means "a function that takes a Dish and returns a Problem, or null". Problem is a small data class that says which check said no, and about which dish. You can keep such a function in a val or a list, pass it as an argument, and return it from another function, just as you'd handle an Int. That's what people mean by functions as values.

Java
// Java has no function types; it uses an interface with one method
Function<Dish, Problem> readyInAnHour =
        d -> d.minutes() > 60 ? new Problem("too-slow", d.name()) : null;
List<Function<Dish, Problem>> everyone = List.of(readyInAnHour, autumnOnly);
Problem p = readyInAnHour.apply(dish);
Kotlin
typealias Check = (Dish) -> Problem?

val readyInAnHour: Check = { d -> if (d.minutes > 60) Problem("too-slow", d.name) else null }
val everyone: List<Check> = listOf(readyInAnHour, autumnOnly)
val p = readyInAnHour(dish)

The { d -> ... } part is a lambda: a function written right where you need it, with no name, its parameters before the arrow and its body after.

Now the code that checks a dish doesn't know any check. It runs a list: checks.firstNotNullOfOrNull { check -> check(dish) }, which calls each check in turn and stops at the first one that returns a problem. Sam is vegetarian, so Sam's list is everyone + meatFree. The demo runs four dishes past both lists:

pumpkin soup: everyone=ok, Sam=ok
slow roast: everyone=too-slow, Sam=too-slow
leek and bacon tart: everyone=ok, Sam=has-meat
strawberry cake: everyone=out-of-season, Sam=out-of-season

The tart is fine for everyone except Sam, and adding Sam's check changed no other line. The strawberry cake fails because this kitchen cooks in autumn, and the strawberries are five months late.

The two languages spell all this differently. Java has no function types, so it uses a functional interface, an interface with one abstract method: Function<T, R>, Predicate<T>, Supplier<T>, or one of your own. You call it by its method name, apply or test.

Kotlin has real function types, and you call a value of one like a function: readyInAnHour(dish). On the JVM, Kotlin's (Dish) -> Problem? is the interface kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<Dish, Problem>, and the call goes to its invoke method. The typealias only gives the type a short name. It creates nothing new.

A check you can hold can be tested, reordered and chosen per guest. Make it a value.

The card in the drawer holds up well so far: store it, lend it, line it up. The picture breaks in one place, and we'll reach it in the last section. First, a lambda is only one of the ways to make a card.

try.title: Add a check without touching the others
steps: Run ChecksAsValues (or ChecksAsValuesJava). Predict first: which dish gets a different answer for Sam?

Alex can't eat nuts. Add a check, val noNuts: Check = { d -> if (d.nuts) Problem("has-nuts", d.name) else null }, and a list, val forAlex = listOf(noNuts) + everyone. Print the answer for the strawberry cake under forAlex. (Java: a NO_NUTS field, and Stream.concat(Stream.of(NO_NUTS), EVERYONE.stream()).toList() for the list.)
Note what you didn't touch: firstProblem and every other check.

code.title: ChecksAsValues.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo data class Dish(val name: String, val minutes: Int, val diet: String, val main: String, val nuts: Boolean = false) data class Problem(val check: String, val dish: String) // A check is a function from a dish to a problem, or null when the dish passes. typealias Check = (Dish) -> Problem? // Each check is a value: a lambda stored in a val, ready to go into a list. val readyInAnHour: Check = { d -> if (d.minutes > 60) Problem("too-slow", d.name) else null } val autumnOnly: Check = { d -> if (d.main in setOf("pumpkin", "leek", "apple", "mushroom")) null else Problem("out-of-season", d.name) } val meatFree: Check = { d -> if (d.diet == "meat") Problem("has-meat", d.name) else null } // Different guests get different lists. Adding a check for one guest changes nothing above. val everyone: List<Check> = listOf(readyInAnHour, autumnOnly) val forSam: List<Check> = everyone + meatFree // Sam is vegetarian // Run the checks in order and stop at the first problem. fun firstProblem(d: Dish, checks: List<Check>): Problem? = checks.firstNotNullOfOrNull { check -> check(d) } fun main() { val dishes = listOf( Dish("pumpkin soup", 40, "vegan", "pumpkin"), Dish("slow roast", 180, "meat", "beef"), Dish("leek and bacon tart", 50, "meat", "leek"), Dish("strawberry cake", 45, "vegetarian", "strawberry", nuts = true), ) for (d in dishes) { val all = firstProblem(d, everyone)?.check ?: "ok" val sam = firstProblem(d, forSam)?.check ?: "ok" println("${d.name}: everyone=$all, Sam=$sam") } }

alt.title: ChecksAsValuesJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.function.Function; /** Java twin of ChecksAsValues.kt. A check is a Function<Dish, Problem> that returns null when the dish passes. */ public class ChecksAsValuesJava { record Dish(String name, int minutes, String diet, String main, boolean nuts) {} record Problem(String check, String dish) {} // Each check is a value: a lambda stored in a field, ready to go into a list. static final Function<Dish, Problem> READY_IN_AN_HOUR = d -> d.minutes() > 60 ? new Problem("too-slow", d.name()) : null; static final Function<Dish, Problem> AUTUMN_ONLY = d -> Set.of("pumpkin", "leek", "apple", "mushroom").contains(d.main()) ? null : new Problem("out-of-season", d.name()); static final Function<Dish, Problem> MEAT_FREE = d -> d.diet().equals("meat") ? new Problem("has-meat", d.name()) : null; // Different guests get different lists. Adding a check for one guest changes nothing above. static final List<Function<Dish, Problem>> EVERYONE = List.of(READY_IN_AN_HOUR, AUTUMN_ONLY); static final List<Function<Dish, Problem>> FOR_SAM = plus(EVERYONE, MEAT_FREE); // Sam is vegetarian static <T> List<T> plus(List<T> list, T extra) { List<T> copy = new ArrayList<>(list); copy.add(extra); return List.copyOf(copy); } // Run the checks in order and stop at the first problem. A check is called with apply. static Problem firstProblem(Dish d, List<Function<Dish, Problem>> checks) { for (Function<Dish, Problem> check : checks) { Problem p = check.apply(d); if (p != null) return p; } return null; } static String name(Problem p) { return p == null ? "ok" : p.check(); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Dish> dishes = List.of( new Dish("pumpkin soup", 40, "vegan", "pumpkin", false), new Dish("slow roast", 180, "meat", "beef", false), new Dish("leek and bacon tart", 50, "meat", "leek", false), new Dish("strawberry cake", 45, "vegetarian", "strawberry", true)); for (Dish d : dishes) { System.out.println(d.name() + ": everyone=" + name(firstProblem(d, EVERYONE)) + ", Sam=" + name(firstProblem(d, FOR_SAM))); } } }

try.expect: The leek and bacon tart passes for everyone and gets has-meat for Sam. Under forAlex, the strawberry cake gets has-nuts instead of out-of-season: the order of the list is the order of the checks, and the first problem wins. firstProblem didn't change, because it never knew any check.

refs.title: Higher-order functions and lambdas: function types (Kotlin docs)

sections.h: Four ways to write a function value: lambdas, references and the rest
sections.html:
A lambda is the most common way to write a function value, but it's one of four. All four below have the same type, and all four ask the same question: does this dish take more than an hour?

Java
Predicate<Integer> lambda = minutes -> minutes > 60;
Predicate<Integer> anon = new Predicate<>() {                 // anonymous class
    public boolean test(Integer minutes) { return minutes > 60; }
};
Predicate<Integer> ref = Timing::isTooSlow;                    // method reference
Predicate<Integer> obj = new TooSlow(60);                      // class implementing Predicate
Kotlin
val lambda: (Int) -> Boolean = { minutes -> minutes > 60 }
val anon: (Int) -> Boolean = fun(minutes: Int): Boolean { return minutes > 60 }
val ref: (Int) -> Boolean = ::isTooSlow                        // function reference
val obj: (Int) -> Boolean = TooSlow(60)                        // class TooSlow : (Int) -> Boolean

A lambda with one parameter can leave it unnamed and use it: { it > 60 }. Its value is its last expression. That's also why a bare return inside a lambda doesn't compile ('return' is prohibited here.): return belongs to the enclosing fun, not to the lambda.

If you want early exits, write an anonymous function, the fun(minutes: Int) form above, where return means what it means everywhere else. Or use a labelled return, return@label, which leaves only the lambda. The demo's anonymous function uses its early exit to flag negative times, because a dish that takes minus five minutes is a typo, not a miracle.

A function reference turns a named function into a value. ::isTooSlow points at a top-level function. Dish::isVegan is unbound: its type takes the receiver as the first parameter, (Dish) -> Boolean. oven::adjust is bound to one oven object, so its type has only the remaining parameters. ::Problem points at the constructor.

Two more shapes show up in Kotlin APIs. A function type can be nullable: ((Problem) -> Unit)? is an optional callback, a function the caller may pass to hear about a problem, or leave out. Mind the parentheses. Without them, (Problem) -> Unit? is a function that returns Unit?. You call a nullable one with onProblem?.invoke(p).

And a function type can have a receiver, a value the lambda sees as this. In Int.() -> Boolean, the body sees the Int as this, so { this % 15 == 0 } asks "is this a whole quarter of an hour?". Receivers are how apply and buildList work. Lesson 6 of this track covers the scope functions, and the Advanced Kotlin track has a lesson on type-safe DSLs. Java has neither: a Consumer<Problem> parameter may simply be null by convention, and there is no receiver.

Four spellings, one type. They don't cost the same, though, and the next question is what each one becomes when it runs.

try.title: Four ways, one type
steps: Open FourWays.kt (or FourWaysJava.java). Predict the four booleans it prints for 45, 90 and -5 minutes.

In tooSlowLambda, add the same early exit the anonymous function has: if (minutes < 0) return true on its own line before minutes > 60. Run it and read the error. Then fix it with a label: write slow@{ minutes -> ... } and return@slow true.

code.title: FourWays.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo // The same "does this dish take too long?" check, written four ways. All four have the type (Int) -> Boolean. // 1. A lambda. val tooSlowLambda: (Int) -> Boolean = { minutes -> minutes > 60 } // 2. An anonymous function. Same type, but `return` means "return from this function". val tooSlowAnon: (Int) -> Boolean = fun(minutes: Int): Boolean { if (minutes < 0) return true // a negative time is a typo, so flag it too return minutes > 60 } // 3. A reference to an ordinary function. fun isTooSlow(minutes: Int): Boolean = minutes > 60 val tooSlowRef: (Int) -> Boolean = ::isTooSlow // 4. A class that implements the function type. class TooSlow(private val maxMinutes: Int) : (Int) -> Boolean { override fun invoke(minutes: Int): Boolean = minutes > maxMinutes } // A function type with a receiver: inside the lambda, `this` is the Int. val isQuarterHour: Int.() -> Boolean = { this % 15 == 0 } // A nullable function type: the caller may pass no callback at all. fun check(minutes: Int, rule: (Int) -> Boolean, onHit: ((Int) -> Unit)? = null): Boolean { val hit = rule(minutes) if (hit) onHit?.invoke(minutes) return hit } fun main() { val rules = listOf(tooSlowLambda, tooSlowAnon, tooSlowRef, TooSlow(60)) for (minutes in listOf(45, 90, -5)) println("$minutes -> ${rules.map { rule -> rule(minutes) }}") println("45.isQuarterHour() = ${45.isQuarterHour()}, 50.isQuarterHour() = ${50.isQuarterHour()}") check(90, tooSlowRef) { println("callback: $it minutes is too slow") } println("no callback given: ${check(90, tooSlowRef)}") }

alt.title: FourWaysJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.IntConsumer; import java.util.function.Predicate; /** * Java twin of FourWays.kt. Java has no function types, so each value is an instance of a functional * interface, here Predicate<Integer>. Java has no receiver types either: Kotlin's Int.() -> Boolean has no twin. */ public class FourWaysJava { // 1. A lambda. static final Predicate<Integer> TOO_SLOW_LAMBDA = minutes -> minutes > 60; // 2. An anonymous class: the closest Java has to an anonymous function. `return` leaves test(). static final Predicate<Integer> TOO_SLOW_ANON = new Predicate<>() { @Override public boolean test(Integer minutes) { if (minutes < 0) return true; // a negative time is a typo, so flag it too return minutes > 60; } }; // 3. A method reference to an ordinary method. static boolean isTooSlow(Integer minutes) { return minutes > 60; } static final Predicate<Integer> TOO_SLOW_REF = FourWaysJava::isTooSlow; // 4. A class that implements the interface. static final class TooSlow implements Predicate<Integer> { private final int maxMinutes; TooSlow(int maxMinutes) { this.maxMinutes = maxMinutes; } @Override public boolean test(Integer minutes) { return minutes > maxMinutes; } } // An optional callback: Java can't say "nullable" in the type, so null is just allowed by convention. static boolean check(int minutes, Predicate<Integer> rule, IntConsumer onHit) { boolean hit = rule.test(minutes); if (hit && onHit != null) onHit.accept(minutes); return hit; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Predicate<Integer>> rules = List.of(TOO_SLOW_LAMBDA, TOO_SLOW_ANON, TOO_SLOW_REF, new TooSlow(60)); for (int minutes : new int[] {45, 90, -5}) { System.out.println(minutes + " -> " + rules.stream().map(rule -> rule.test(minutes)).toList()); } check(90, TOO_SLOW_REF, m -> System.out.println("callback: " + m + " minutes is too slow")); System.out.println("no callback given: " + check(90, TOO_SLOW_REF, null)); } }

try.expect: 45 prints four false, 90 four true. For -5 only the anonymous function says true, because it is the only one with the early return. The bare return in the lambda fails with 'return' is prohibited here.; the labelled return@slow true returns from the lambda and compiles. The Java version has no isQuarterHour line, because Java has no receiver types.

sections.h: What a lambda turns into on the JVM, and what it costs
sections.html:
A function value is an object, so something has to create it. What that costs depends on how you wrote it, and Kotlin and Java don't agree on every case.

Since Kotlin 2.0, lambdas compile to invokedynamic by default, the mechanism Java has used for lambdas since Java 8. invokedynamic is a bytecode instruction (one step of the JVM's own machine language) that asks a helper method, the first time it runs, how to do its job.

The compiler moves the lambda body into a private static method, such as nonCapturing$lambda$0. Where the lambda is created, it emits an invokedynamic whose helper is LambdaMetafactory.metafactory. The first time that instruction runs, the JVM spins up a hidden class that implements Function1 and calls the private method. No .class file for the lambda shows up in your build output. (Kotlin 1.x generated one class per lambda, and the compiler flag -Xlambdas=class still brings that back.)

How many objects you get depends on what the lambda captures, that is, which variables from outside its body it uses. The demo's capturing(extra) returns { it + extra }, a card with a note pinned to it, while nonCapturing() returns { it + 10 }, which needs nothing from outside:

Java
nonCapturing() == nonCapturing();       // true on HotSpot: one shared instance
capturing(5) == capturing(5);           // false: a new object per evaluation
Kotlin
nonCapturing() === nonCapturing()       // true: one shared instance
capturing(5) === capturing(5)           // false: a new object per evaluation
capturing(5) == capturing(5)            // false: lambdas have no equals

A non-capturing lambda uses nothing from outside its body, so one instance serves every call. A capturing lambda holds the values it uses (extra here), so each evaluation allocates a new object with those values inside. On JDK 21, the demo printed this for Kotlin (the number after 0x changes from run to run):

non-capturing lambda: same object every time?  true
capturing lambda: same object every time?      false
capturing lambdas equal with == ?              false
unbound reference ::addRest: same object?      true
bound reference oven::adjust: same object?     false

lambda class:    workbench.functional.l02.demo.LambdaShapesKt$$Lambda/0x00000007c0001800  (hidden: true)
reference class: workbench.functional.l02.demo.LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1  (hidden: false, extends FunctionReferenceImpl)

The shared instance for a non-capturing lambda is what HotSpot does today, not a promise. Don't write code that depends on it.

The last line is where Kotlin differs from Java. In Kotlin 2.4.21, function references such as ::addRest and oven::adjust still compile to real classes, LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1 and LambdaShapesKt$boundRef$1, which extend kotlin.jvm.internal.FunctionReferenceImpl. An unbound reference is a singleton held in a static INSTANCE field. A bound one is a new object each time, holding its receiver. Java method references go through invokedynamic like lambdas do, and leave no class file behind.

One more cost hides in the types. (Long) -> Long is Function1<Long, Long>, which is generic, so a call through it boxes the long: it wraps the number in a java.lang.Long object and unwraps it again. Java avoids that with primitive interfaces like LongUnaryOperator. Kotlin has no primitive function interfaces. It avoids the box another way, with inline functions, which the next lesson covers.

None of this is a reason to avoid lambdas. A capturing lambda costs one small object per evaluation, which the JVM allocates cheaply. It starts to matter in two places: a capturing lambda created inside a hot loop, and code that compares function values with ==, which never works for lambdas.

Objects are cheap. The surprise is what happens to a captured variable that changes.

try.title: Count the objects and the class files
steps: Run LambdaShapes (or LambdaShapesJava). Before you look, predict the five true or false answers.
From labs/, list the compiled demo classes: ls functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/functional/l02/demo/. Look for a class per lambda and a class per reference.
Run javap -c -p functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/functional/l02/demo/LambdaShapesKt.class and find the first instruction of nonCapturing and of topLevelRef.

code.title: LambdaShapes.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo fun addRest(minutes: Long): Long = minutes + 10 // let it rest 10 minutes fun nonCapturing(): (Long) -> Long = { it + 10 } // uses nothing from outside fun capturing(extra: Long): (Long) -> Long = { it + extra } // captures extra fun topLevelRef(): (Long) -> Long = ::addRest // a function reference class Oven(private val extraMinutes: Long) { // this oven runs a little cold fun adjust(minutes: Long): Long = minutes + extraMinutes } fun boundRef(o: Oven): (Long) -> Long = o::adjust // a reference bound to one object fun main() { val oven = Oven(5) println("non-capturing lambda: same object every time? ${nonCapturing() === nonCapturing()}") println("capturing lambda: same object every time? ${capturing(5) === capturing(5)}") println("capturing lambdas equal with == ? ${capturing(5) == capturing(5)}") println("unbound reference ::addRest: same object? ${topLevelRef() === topLevelRef()}") println("bound reference oven::adjust: same object? ${boundRef(oven) === boundRef(oven)}") println() val lambda = nonCapturing().javaClass val ref = topLevelRef().javaClass println("lambda class: ${lambda.name} (hidden: ${lambda.isHidden})") println("reference class: ${ref.name} (hidden: ${ref.isHidden}, extends ${ref.superclass.simpleName})") }

alt.title: LambdaShapesJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo; import java.util.function.LongUnaryOperator; /** * Java twin of LambdaShapes.kt. In Java both lambdas and method references go through invokedynamic, * so neither leaves a class file behind. Compare the last two lines with the Kotlin version. */ public class LambdaShapesJava { static long addRest(long minutes) { return minutes + 10; } // let it rest 10 minutes static LongUnaryOperator nonCapturing() { return m -> m + 10; } // uses nothing from outside static LongUnaryOperator capturing(long extra) { return m -> m + extra; } // captures extra static LongUnaryOperator staticRef() { return LambdaShapesJava::addRest; } // a method reference static final class ColdOven { // this oven runs a little cold private final long extraMinutes; ColdOven(long extraMinutes) { this.extraMinutes = extraMinutes; } long adjust(long minutes) { return minutes + extraMinutes; } } static LongUnaryOperator boundRef(ColdOven o) { return o::adjust; } // bound to one object public static void main(String[] args) { ColdOven oven = new ColdOven(5); System.out.println("non-capturing lambda: same object every time? " + (nonCapturing() == nonCapturing())); System.out.println("capturing lambda: same object every time? " + (capturing(5) == capturing(5))); System.out.println("capturing lambdas equal with equals? " + capturing(5).equals(capturing(5))); System.out.println("static method ref: same object? " + (staticRef() == staticRef())); System.out.println("bound method ref oven::adjust: same object? " + (boundRef(oven) == boundRef(oven))); System.out.println(); Class<?> lambda = nonCapturing().getClass(); Class<?> ref = staticRef().getClass(); System.out.println("lambda class: " + lambda.getName() + " (hidden: " + lambda.isHidden() + ")"); System.out.println("method ref class: " + ref.getName() + " (hidden: " + ref.isHidden() + ")"); } }

try.expect: true, false, false, true, false in both languages. The Kotlin lambda's class is a hidden class named like LambdaShapesKt$$Lambda/0x..., while the reference's class is an ordinary class, LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1, that extends FunctionReferenceImpl. The directory has LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1.class and LambdaShapesKt$boundRef$1.class, and no file for any lambda. In the Java version, the lambda and the method reference are both hidden classes. javap shows invokedynamic ... invoke:()Lkotlin/jvm/functions/Function1; in nonCapturing and getstatic ... LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1.INSTANCE in topLevelRef.

refs.title: What's new in Kotlin 2.0.0: lambdas via invokedynamic

sections.h: A closure keeps its variables, and a captured var becomes one shared box
sections.html:
A lambda can use variables from the function that created it, and it keeps them after that function has returned. Code plus the variables it captured is called a closure. It's the recipe card with a note pinned to it: "my oven runs hot, take five minutes off". The note was written where the card was made, and it goes wherever the card goes.

Java
static IntSupplier makeCounter() {
    int[] count = {0};                  // Java makes you build the box yourself
    return () -> ++count[0];
}
Kotlin
fun makeCounter(): () -> Int {
    var count = 0
    return { ++count }                  // the lambda keeps count alive
}

Call makeCounter() twice and you get two counters, each with its own count. Each one returns 1, 2, 3 and so on.

Look at what the Java version needed. Java refuses to capture a local variable that changes: local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final. The reason is mechanical. A local variable lives in the method's stack frame, the memory one method call uses for its locals, and that frame is gone once makeCounter returns.

The lambda outlives the frame, so all it can take is a copy of the value, and copying a variable that keeps changing would be confusing. Java programmers work around it with a one-element array or an AtomicInteger. Either one is an object on the heap, the memory where objects live for as long as something points at them, and both sides can share it.

Kotlin builds that object for you, silently. When a lambda captures a var, the compiler moves the variable into a small heap object, a kotlin.jvm.internal.Ref$IntRef (or LongRef, ObjectRef and so on). Both the function and the lambda use its field. The field is a plain public int element, with no volatile and no lock. Java refuses the capture; the Kotlin compiler shrugs and builds the box.

Here the recipe card picture breaks, and it breaks in a way that matters. Lend a paper card and your friend gets their own copy of the note. Hand out a closure and everyone holds the same box.

That's fine on one thread. It's a bug as soon as two threads share the closure. A thread is one path of work through a program, and several can run at the same moment. ++count becomes "read element, add one, write element", the same read-modify-write as count++ in the race conditions lesson. When two threads read the same old value, one of the two additions is lost. Nothing in the Kotlin source looks shared. The sharing comes from the box the compiler made.

The CapturedRace demo shares one captured var total between four tasks on a thread pool (a fixed group of threads that take tasks from a queue). Each task adds 1 a quarter of a million times, and the whole thing runs ten times. One try on this busy 4-core machine began like this:

run  1: expected 1,000,000, got   250,956 (lost 749,044)
run  2: expected 1,000,000, got 1,000,000 (lost 0)
run  3: expected 1,000,000, got 1,000,000 (lost 0)

Runs 4 to 10 were correct too. A second try lost 202,126 in run 1, and a third lost nothing in all ten. The Java twin, with its hand-made array box, lost exactly 500,000 in one run.

Most losses land in the first run, while the JVM is still interpreting the loop. Then the JIT compiler, the part of the JVM that turns busy code into machine code, compiles it. From then on each task keeps the count in a register, a slot inside the processor, and writes it back once at the end. Then a loss wipes out whole tasks, which is why 500,000 is such a round number. The memory model track explains why the JIT may do that to a plain field. A race that shows up once in ten runs is still a race, and the worst kind, because it passes most tests.

A captured var is one box that everyone holding the closure shares. Never change it from two threads.

There are two fixes. Share a thread-safe object instead of a var: capture val total = AtomicLong() and call total.incrementAndGet(). Or, better, don't share at all. Let each task count its own work and combine the results at the end with a sum or a fold. The second fix is the functional one, and it keeps working when the tasks move to other machines.

That second fix needs functions that take other functions and combine their results. Writing our own is where the next lesson starts.

try.title: Lose updates, then fix it two ways
steps: Run CapturedRace (or CapturedRaceJava). Four pool threads each add 1 to a captured total 250,000 times, ten runs in a row. If all ten runs print 1,000,000, run it once more: the losses come and go.
Fix it by sharing a thread-safe object: make it val total = AtomicLong() (Java: AtomicLong total = new AtomicLong()), call total.incrementAndGet() in the loop, and print total.get(). Run it.

Undo that, and fix it by not sharing: make each task return its own count, pool.submit(Callable { go.await(); var mine = 0L; repeat(250_000) { mine += 1 }; mine }), then add up tasks.sumOf { it.get() }. (Java: return mine from the lambda and add up the Future<Long> results.) Run it.

code.title: CapturedRace.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors // Four pool threads add to one captured var. The var lives in a Ref.LongRef box with a plain field. fun main() { val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4) repeat(10) { run -> var total = 0L // captured below, so it becomes a Ref.LongRef val go = CountDownLatch(1) // start all four tasks at the same moment val tasks = List(4) { pool.submit { go.await() repeat(250_000) { total += 1 } // read element, add 1, write element } } go.countDown() tasks.forEach { it.get() } println("run %2d: expected 1,000,000, got %,9d (lost %,d)".format(run + 1, total, 1_000_000 - total)) } pool.shutdown() }

alt.title: CapturedRaceJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l02.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** * Java twin of CapturedRace.kt. Java refuses to capture a local that changes: * long total = 0; ... () -> total += 1 * error: local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final * So Java programmers write the box by hand, a one-element array. That is what Kotlin's Ref.LongRef is. */ public class CapturedRaceJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); for (int run = 1; run <= 10; run++) { long[] total = {0}; // the hand-made box: a plain array slot CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); // start all four tasks at the same moment List<Future<?>> tasks = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 4; t++) { tasks.add(pool.submit(() -> { go.await(); for (int i = 0; i < 250_000; i++) total[0] += 1; // read, add 1, write return null; })); } go.countDown(); for (Future<?> f : tasks) f.get(); System.out.printf("run %2d: expected 1,000,000, got %,9d (lost %,d)%n", run, total[0], 1_000_000 - total[0]); } pool.shutdown(); } }

try.expect: The broken version loses updates in some runs, by different amounts each time, most often in run 1. Here one try lost 749,044 in run 1 and nothing after, and another lost nothing in all ten runs. Both fixes print exactly 1,000,000 in every run, every try. The don't-share version has no contention at all: mine is only ever touched by one thread, so the compiler keeps it a plain local (repeat is inline, so no lambda captures it).

compare.title: Checks and closures with functional interfaces and with function types

java.title: Checks.java
java.html: import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Function; import java.util.function.IntSupplier; record Dish(String name, int minutes, String diet) {} record Problem(String check, String dish) {} final class Checks { // a function value is an instance of a functional interface static Function<Dish, Problem> readyWithin(int maxMinutes) { return d -> d.minutes() > maxMinutes ? new Problem("too-slow", d.name()) : null; // captures maxMinutes } static Problem firstProblem(Dish d, List<Function<Dish, Problem>> checks) { return checks.stream() .map(check -> check.apply(d)) // called by its method name .filter(p -> p != null) .findFirst() .orElse(null); } // a captured local that changes is a compile error; the array is the box, built by hand static IntSupplier makeCounter() { int[] count = {0}; return () -> ++count[0]; } }

kotlin.title: Checks.kt
kotlin.html: data class Dish(val name: String, val minutes: Int, val diet: String) data class Problem(val check: String, val dish: String) typealias Check = (Dish) -> Problem? // a real function type: Function1 on the JVM fun readyWithin(maxMinutes: Int): Check = { d -> // captures maxMinutes if (d.minutes > maxMinutes) Problem("too-slow", d.name) else null } fun firstProblem(d: Dish, checks: List<Check>): Problem? = checks.firstNotNullOfOrNull { check -> check(d) } // called like a function // capturing a var is allowed; the compiler builds the Ref box for you fun makeCounter(): () -> Int { var count = 0 return { ++count } }

compare.note: Kotlin has function types; Java has functional interfaces. That changes three things you notice every day. Kotlin calls a function value with f(x), where Java needs the interface's method name (apply, test, getAsInt), and Kotlin has one family of types, (A) -> B, where Java has dozens of interfaces, primitive ones included. Kotlin's types can say "may be null" (Problem?, ((Problem) -> Unit)?), so a check that returns null shows it in its type. And Kotlin lets a lambda capture a var by moving it into a Ref box, where Java insists on effectively final locals and makes you write the box. Under the hood both compile lambdas with invokedynamic; only Kotlin's function references still compile to classes.

worked.title: Find the hidden shared box in a recipe import

steps.say: A recipe app imports a big file of recipes. It splits the list into chunks of 500 with chunked(500), saves each chunk on a thread pool, and counts how many recipes it saved. Under load the count comes out a little low, and only sometimes. Find the shared state before reading on.
steps.code: fun importAll(recipes: List<Recipe>, pool: ExecutorService): Int { var saved = 0 val futures = recipes.chunked(500).map { chunk -> pool.submit { chunk.forEach { r -> if (book.save(r)) saved += 1 } } } futures.forEach { it.get() } return saved }

alt.html: // The Java version doesn't compile as written: static int importAll(List<Recipe> recipes, ExecutorService pool) throws Exception { int saved = 0; List<Future<?>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (List<Recipe> chunk : chunks(recipes, 500)) { futures.add(pool.submit(() -> { for (Recipe r : chunk) if (book.save(r)) saved += 1; // error: local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final })); } for (Future<?> f : futures) f.get(); return saved; }

steps.say: 1. Find the box. saved is a var captured by the lambda passed to submit, which runs on pool threads. The compiler turned it into one Ref$IntRef, and every chunk task does read, add, write on its plain element field. (forEach is inline, so its lambda doesn't count; the submit lambda is the one that captures.) Java refused the same code, and the usual Java workaround is the same box written by hand.
steps.code: // roughly what the compiler made of it val saved = Ref.IntRef() // one box on the heap pool.submit { ...; saved.element += 1 } // every task, on every thread

alt.html: int[] saved = {0}; // the box Java makes you write pool.submit(() -> { ...; saved[0] += 1; }); // the same race

steps.say: 1. Don't share. Make each task count its own saves in a local, return that count, and add the counts up on the calling thread. Each task's lambda now captures only its chunk, which nobody changes. Self-check: why is the var mine inside the task safe? (It's a local of that one task, used on one thread, and no other lambda captures it, so it never becomes a box.)
steps.code: fun importAll(recipes: List<Recipe>, pool: ExecutorService): Int { val futures = recipes.chunked(500).map { chunk -> pool.submit(Callable { // 1. each task returns a value var mine = 0 // a local: only this task touches it for (r in chunk) if (book.save(r)) mine++ mine }) } return futures.sumOf { it.get() } // 2. combine on one thread }

alt.html: static int importAll(List<Recipe> recipes, ExecutorService pool) throws Exception { List<Future<Integer>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (List<Recipe> chunk : chunks(recipes, 500)) { futures.add(pool.submit(() -> { // 1. each task returns a value int mine = 0; // a local: only this task touches it for (Recipe r : chunk) if (book.save(r)) mine++; return mine; })); } int total = 0; for (Future<Integer> f : futures) total += f.get(); // 2. combine on one thread return total; }

steps.say: 1. If you do need a live shared number, say a progress bar while the import runs, share a thread-safe object through a val, never a var. LongAdder spreads the work over several cells and is cheaper than AtomicLong when many threads add at once.
steps.code: val savedSoFar = LongAdder() // a val: the reference never changes pool.submit { chunk.forEach { r -> if (book.save(r)) savedSoFar.increment() } }

alt.html: LongAdder savedSoFar = new LongAdder(); // effectively final, so Java is happy too pool.submit(() -> { for (Recipe r : chunk) if (book.save(r)) savedSoFar.increment(); });

lab.title: Checks as values, and a counter that survives eight threads
steps: Open Checks.kt. A Dish has a name, the minutes it takes, a diet and a main ingredient, and a Check is a (Dish) -> Problem?. Run the tests. All ten fail: nine with NotImplementedError, and the shared-counter test with a short count, something like but was: 1580389L where 1,600,001 was expected.
Write readyWithin (return a lambda that captures maxMinutes), meatFree (a lambda in a val) and inSeason. Then replace the body of seasonCheck with the reference ::inSeason.
Write firstProblem and allProblems. firstProblem must stop at the first problem: one test counts calls to a later check that phones a guest.
Write suits. The callback is optional, so call it with ?.invoke.
In Counters.kt, write makeCounter. Then fix makeSharedCounter so the 8-thread test passes. Keep the return type () -> Long.
Run the tests until all ten pass, then run them twice more. A race fix has to pass every time.
hints: checks.firstNotNullOfOrNull { check -> check(dish) } returns the first non-null result and stops there. mapNotNull keeps every non-null result.
If meatFree gives you a type error, name the lambda's parameter and make both branches of the if produce a Problem?: { d -> if (d.diet in MEAT_FREE_DIETS) null else Problem(...) }.
A val that holds an AtomicLong is safe to capture: the reference never changes, and incrementAndGet() is one atomic step that returns the new value.
lab.done: All ten tests in FunctionValuesTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write two closures from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write scaleFor(guests, serves), which returns a function from grams to grams: a recipe that serves serves people, scaled for guests, so grams * guests / serves. Then write makeCounter(), and add a one-line comment saying what the compiler does with its captured var. Write both in Kotlin and in Java, and note the one line Java refuses to compile.

answer.html: fun scaleFor(guests: Int, serves: Int): (Int) -> Int = { grams -> grams * guests / serves } // captures guests and serves fun makeCounter(): () -> Int { var count = 0 // captured var: moved into a Ref.IntRef box with a plain int field return { ++count } } // val forSix = scaleFor(6, 4) // forSix(200) == 300, forSix(250) == 375 // val c = makeCounter(); c(); c() == 2

alt.html: static IntUnaryOperator scaleFor(int guests, int serves) { return grams -> grams * guests / serves; } static IntSupplier makeCounter() { // int count = 0; return () -> ++count; <- won't compile: // local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final int[] count = {0}; // the box, written by hand return () -> ++count[0]; }

recap: A function type such as (Dish) -> Problem? is a type like any other: store its values, put them in lists, pass them and return them. On the JVM it is Function1.
Java uses functional interfaces (Function, Predicate, your own) and calls them by method name. Kotlin calls a function value like a function.
Lambdas, anonymous functions, references and classes that implement a function type all make function values. A bare return is prohibited in a lambda that isn't inlined.

Kotlin 2.x compiles lambdas with invokedynamic: no class file, one shared instance when nothing is captured, a new object per evaluation when something is. Function references still compile to classes.
A closure keeps the variables it captured. A captured var lives in one Ref box with a plain field, and everyone holding the closure shares it.
The limit: a closure is only as safe to share as what it captured. Return a value from each task and combine the values, or capture a val that holds an atomic.

explain.prompt: A teammate's Kotlin counter, a var n = 0 captured by a lambda that four threads call, loses counts. They say: "There's no shared field anywhere in my code." Explain what the compiler did and what you would change.
explain.answer: A local variable normally lives in the stack frame of the function that declares it, and the lambda outlives that frame. So when a lambda captures a var, Kotlin moves the variable into a small object on the heap, a Ref$IntRef, and both the function and the lambda use its element field. That field is the shared field: all four threads reach it through the same lambda. It's a plain field, so n++ is a read, an add and a write that two threads can interleave, and increments get lost. Java would have refused to compile the capture. I'd stop sharing: have each thread or task count its own work and add the counts up at the end. If a live shared count is needed, I'd capture a val holding a LongAdder or AtomicLong instead of a var.

deeper.html:
javap -v shows how invokedynamic is wired. Each lambda site has an entry in the class's BootstrapMethods table pointing at LambdaMetafactory.metafactory, with three arguments: the erased method type of invoke, (Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Object;, a handle to the private static method holding the body, and the instantiated type, (Ljava/lang/Long;)Ljava/lang/Long; for a (Long) -> Long. The erased signature is why a call through Function1 boxes: invoke takes and returns Object.

Kotlin 2.0's switch to invokedynamic changed three visible things, according to its release notes. These lambdas aren't serializable, the experimental reflect() API doesn't support them, and toString() prints the hidden class name, something like LambdaShapesKt$$Lambda/0x...@1b6d3586, instead of a readable description of the function type. A test or log that matched on the old text breaks after the upgrade. Annotate a single lambda with @JvmSerializableLambda, or compile the module with -Xlambdas=class, to get the old class-per-lambda behaviour.

SAM conversions went to invokedynamic earlier, in Kotlin 1.5. A SAM conversion turns a lambda into an instance of an interface with a Single Abstract Method: a Kotlin lambda passed where Java expects a Runnable or Comparator, or a lambda for your own fun interface:

Java
@FunctionalInterface
interface Rest { int minutesFor(int grams); }

Rest flat = grams -> 10;                      // Java lambdas have always worked this way
Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("timer done");
Kotlin
fun interface Rest { fun minutesFor(grams: Int): Int }

val flat = Rest { 10 }                       // a SAM conversion: invokedynamic, no class file
val task = Runnable { println("timer done") } // the same for a Java interface

A fun interface is worth using when a function type needs a name in a public API, or when Java callers will implement it, since Java code can't write a lambda for Function1 as naturally as for an interface named after its job.
